content.text: In 1938, scientists discovered that uranium nuclei could be split apart, releasing enormous amounts of energy. This process—nuclear fission—powers nuclear reactors and, in uncontrolled form, nuclear weapons. Understanding fission is essential for appreciating both the benefits and risks of nuclear technology.

Nuclear fission is the splitting of a large nucleus into two smaller nuclei, releasing neutrons and a large amount of energy. A chain reaction occurs when the neutrons released cause further fission events. In a nuclear reactor, control rods absorb excess neutrons to keep the chain reaction steady.

This 'missing mass' (mass defect) is converted to energy

How a Nuclear Power Station Works
Control rods drop automatically if power fails
Explain why control rods are essential in a nuclear reactor.
Control rods absorb neutrons. By adjusting how far they're inserted:
More inserted = fewer neutrons = slower reaction
Less inserted = more neutrons = faster reaction
This maintains the reaction at a constant rate (critical state). Without control rods, the chain reaction would become uncontrolled, leading to overheating and potential meltdown.
Explain why a moderator is needed in a nuclear reactor.
Neutrons released by fission are fast (high kinetic energy)
Fast neutrons are less likely to cause fission in U-235
The moderator (water or graphite) slows neutrons down
Slow (thermal) neutrons have a higher probability of being absorbed and causing fission
This makes the chain reaction more efficient
Radioactive waste (remains hazardous for thousands of years)

Make sure you can name and describe the function of each reactor component: fuel rods (contain the fissile material), moderator (slows neutrons), control rods (absorb neutrons to control the rate), coolant (transfers heat away), and shielding (protects workers from radiation).

In a controlled chain reaction, exactly one neutron per fission event causes further fission (on average). The control rods absorb the excess neutrons. Raising control rods increases the rate; lowering them decreases it. In an emergency, they are fully inserted to shut down the reactor.
Fission: splitting heavy nucleus into smaller nuclei + neutrons + energy
Common fuel: U-235 (must be enriched from 0.7% to 3-5%)
Chain reaction: neutrons from one fission cause more fissions
Fuel: uranium oxide in fuel rods
Energy from mass defect: E = mc²
Advantages: no CO₂, high energy density
Disadvantages: radioactive waste, accident risk, high costs
Nuclear fission is the splitting of a large, unstable nucleus (such as U-235) into two smaller daughter nuclei, accompanied by the release of two or three neutrons and a large amount of energy.
— definition must include splitting, products, and energy (definition)

In fission, the neutrons released as products can be absorbed by other fissile nuclei, triggering further fissions — each event produces the trigger for the next. In radioactive decay (alpha, beta, gamma), the emitted particles do not cause neighbouring nuclei to decay; decay is spontaneous and independent.
— fission products trigger further reactions; decay products do not (reasoning)

Control rods (made of boron or cadmium) absorb neutrons. Inserting them further into the core removes more neutrons, slowing the chain reaction. Withdrawing them allows more neutrons to cause fissions, increasing the reaction rate. This maintains exactly one neutron per fission causing another fission (critical state).
— neutron absorption regulates chain reaction rate (description)

Natural uranium contains only 0.7% U-235 (the fissile isotope) and 99.3% U-238 (not fissile). At such low concentration, too few neutrons encounter U-235 nuclei to sustain a chain reaction. Enrichment increases U-235 to 3-5%, making the chain reaction self-sustaining.
— insufficient fissile concentration in natural uranium (reasoning)

Controlled fission heats the fuel rods. Coolant (water or gas) carries heat away from the core to a heat exchanger. Water is heated to steam, which drives turbines. The turbines spin generators, which produce electricity by electromagnetic induction.
— thermal energy -> kinetic energy -> electrical energy (description)

Advantages: no CO2 emissions during operation; very high energy density (1 kg U-235 ~ 2000 tonnes coal); reliable baseload power. Disadvantages: produces long-lived radioactive waste requiring secure storage for thousands of years; risk of serious accidents (though rare); high construction and decommissioning costs; nuclear proliferation concerns.
